title: Datoric doubled the countries it collects data from with Dots
summary: Datoric’s contributors in Latin America needed bank transfers. With Dots Payout Links, it went live in about a week and paid in twice as many countries.
body_markdown:
Contributors in Latin America needed bank transfers Datoric couldn’t send through its existing payment apps. With Dots, Datoric expanded its data collection to twice as many countries.


## **Results at a glance**


Result


What changed for Datoric


More than 10x


Contributors paid in its busiest week on Dots, compared with its busiest week paying by hand.


About 5 minutes


Median payout completion after a contributor’s request, compared with about 2.5 hours by hand.

The number of countries where Datoric paid contributors in the month to early October 2026, compared with before Dots.

## **Training data for robotics and physical AI**


Datoric builds training and evaluation data for robotics and physical AI teams, including frontier AI labs. It starts with a model failure or a skill a customer wants its model to learn, then tests how to collect the data needed.


Contributors record data such as first-person video of everyday tasks in homes and workplaces. Datoric works with contributors directly and through collection partners that manage their own teams.


In September 2026, Datoric delivered about 209,000 accepted hours of data and paid eight times as many contributors as in July. Its payment process had to keep up with that growing network.


## **Contributors needed bank transfers the team couldn’t send**


In early July 2026, contributors in Latin America who had joined through a collection partner asked to be paid by bank transfer. Datoric’s process relied on PayPal and other payment apps, and it couldn’t send the transfers they needed.


Datoric depended on those contributors for recordings that met its customers’ quality standards. To keep working with them, it needed a way to pay them where they lived.


> "Contributors stay only if they can receive their money in a way that works where they live, and partners need to pay their own teams on time. – **Jeff Lin, CTO of Datoric**


One of Datoric’s founders handled payments alongside day-to-day operations. Each request meant sending money through an app and marking it paid in Datoric’s system.


Payments sent by hand grew from about 20 a week in June to about 200 in the first full week of July. Contributors waited a median of about 2.5 hours after requesting payment, and one in ten waited 22 hours or more because someone had to be available to send the money.


## **Live in about a week**


Datoric built its Payout Links integration in about four days and went live about a week after starting.


Payout Links let contributors choose from the payment methods available to them, including bank transfer and PayPal. Dots shows the options each person can use, so Datoric didn’t have to build payment rules for each country. Contributors enter their bank and identity details on Dots’ pages, keeping that information out of Datoric’s systems.


Those payment options let Datoric work with contributors its previous process couldn’t pay. The team could expand data collection into new countries through the same integration.


During setup and ongoing use, a shared Slack channel connected Datoric with Dots support.


> “Their support team is quick: in our shared Slack channel, our questions about deposits and payouts were often resolved within hours.” – **Jeff Lin, CTO of Datoric**


## **Collecting data from twice as many countries**


With Dots, Datoric began paying contributors in countries where it had never paid anyone before, opening more places to collect data. In the month to early October 2026, it paid contributors in more than twice as many countries as before Dots.


> "Through Dots we have paid thousands of contributors in a single week without anyone on our team sending payouts by hand." – **Jeff Lin, CTO of Datoric**


By August 2026, Datoric had stopped sending contributor payments by hand, leaving the team to review unusually large payouts and handle exceptions. Dots kept pace as Datoric paid more than ten times as many contributors in its busiest week as it had ever paid by hand in a week.
